title: Thermodynamic Stability of Classical $\mathbb Z_2$ Lattice Gauge Models
authors: Shunsuke Sengoku, Weiguang Cao, Haruki Watanabe
abstract: Finite-temperature phases are traditionally studied through spontaneous symmetry breaking, but symmetry-breaking fields can remove their distinction, as in the Ising model. This motivates the search for stable nontrivial thermal phases without symmetry protection. For classical $\mathbb Z_2$ lattice gauge models with spins on $m$-dimensional cells in a fixed spatial dimension $d$, we prove joint analyticity of the thermodynamic free-energy density in temperature and perturbation strength at sufficiently low positive temperatures under sufficiently weak local perturbations, whenever $1\le m\le d-2$. Perturbations need not preserve internal or gauge symmetries and may include noncommuting quantum interactions. A separate high-temperature expansion yields an analytic region reaching infinite temperature at any fixed finite perturbation strength. These results establish thermodynamic stability and support the conjecture that low- and high-temperature regimes remain separated by a thermal transition without symmetry protection.
summary: This work rigorously proves the thermodynamic stability of classical $\mathbb Z_2$ lattice gauge models by demonstrating the joint analyticity of the free-energy density in temperature and perturbation strength. The key finding is that such stability can be established for dimensions $1 \le m \le d-2$ without relying on spontaneous symmetry breaking. This advances the understanding of thermal phase transitions in lattice gauge theories.
main_problem: The research aims to establish the thermodynamic stability of classical $\mathbb Z_2$ lattice gauge models, particularly proving the existence of stable nontrivial thermal phases that are not protected by spontaneous symmetry breaking.
main_result: The authors prove joint analyticity of the thermodynamic free-energy density in temperature and perturbation strength for $1 \le m \le d-2$, establishing stability without symmetry protection.
method: The analysis employs techniques involving joint analyticity proofs, high-temperature expansions, and gauge averaging to control the free energy density in the thermodynamic limit.
model_or_system: The system is a classical $\mathbb Z_2$ lattice gauge model defined on spins occupying $m$-dimensional cells in a $d$-dimensional lattice. The Hamiltonian involves products of Pauli operators on the boundaries of higher-dimensional cells.
key_observables: Thermodynamic free-energy density ($f$ or $\psi$), and the joint analyticity of this free energy with respect to temperature ($T$ or $\beta$) and perturbation strength ($g$ or $\lambda$).
important_parameters: The dimensions $d$ and $m$, temperature $T$ (or $\beta$), and the perturbation strength $g$. The results are specifically proven for the range $1 \le m \le d-2$.
main_assumptions: The proofs rely on bounding component shapes and placement counts, and the initial results do not cover the entire unperturbed low-temperature phase or prove a singularity separates the low- and high-temperature analytic regions.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically shows the family of spin models based on $m$-cells (vertex, link, plaquette, cube). Figure 2 illustrates phase diagrams for the Ising model and the 3D plaquette model, showing different transition types and analytic domains.
paper_structure: The paper develops the analysis by first defining the model and the problem of stability. It then uses advanced techniques like cluster expansions and complex analysis to prove joint analyticity of the free energy density in both low- and high-temperature regimes, culminating in the establishment of thermodynamic stability.
why_interesting: The rigorous mathematical proof of thermal stability in lattice gauge theories, especially in the absence of symmetry protection, provides deep insights into the nature of quantum phase transitions relevant to condensed matter physics.

Red shading in (b) marks the deconfined regime. Solid red (dark gray) lines denote first-order (continuous) transitions; off-axis filled dots (open circles) denote multicritical points (critical endpoints). (c) Low- (red) and high-temperature (gray) analytic domains of Theorems 1 and 2, restricted to T > 0. Dashed curves mark sufficient bounds, not phase boundaries. White regions are unclassified.
